chief_complaint: throbbing neck pulses, wide pulse pressure, diastolic murmur
hpi_details: A 32-year-old female presents to the clinic with throbbing neck pulses, wide pulse pressure, diastolic murmur. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks the pounding sensation in her neck is caused by intense workplace stress and drinking too many energy drinks while working late.
concerns: She is worried that one of the throbbing blood vessels in her neck might burst or cause a sudden stroke while she is home alone.
expectations: She hopes the doctor can prescribe a calming heart-slowing pill so her neck stops visibly pulsating.

investigation_events.title: Transthoracic echocardiogram
investigation_events.availability_message: The transthoracic echocardiogram report is now available.

results.value: Bicuspid aortic valve with severe eccentric regurgitation; vena contracta 0.7 cm; holodiastolic flow reversal; LV end-systolic diameter 46 mm; LVEF 54%
results.reference_range: No significant regurgitation; vena contracta <0.3 cm

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Aortic Regurgitation (Insufficiency) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes echocardiographic assessment of severity and left-ventricular response, with referral for severe disease according to symptoms and ventricular criteria, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: throbbing neck pulses, wide pulse pressure, diastolic murmur

Key HPI features: A 32-year-old female presents to the clinic with throbbing neck pulses, wide pulse pressure, diastolic murmur. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Aortic Insufficiency.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Aortic Regurgitation (Insufficiency).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Mitral regurgitation without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Declining ejection fraction — surgical threshold for valve replacement.
management_principles: Plan for aortic regurgitation: obtain echocardiography to define severity, left-ventricular size, and function; refer severe disease according to symptoms and ventricular criteria
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of throbbing neck pulses, wide pulse pressure, diastolic murmur. HPI: aortic valve dilation or cusp prolapse.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Aortic Insufficiency.
reference_soap.assessment: Bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure, and a diastolic murmur are consistent with aortic regurgitation; echocardiography is needed to define severity and left ventricular response.
reference_soap.plan: Plan for aortic regurgitation: obtain echocardiography to define severity, left-ventricular size, and function. Refer severe disease for valve evaluation according to symptoms and ventricular criteria, including progressive ventricular dilation or systolic dysfunction; do not rely on ejection-fraction decline alone. Counsel patient.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Aortic Insufficiency
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Aortic Insufficiency
Implement evidence-based management plan: Echocardiogram, refer for surgical valve replacement if EF declines

teaching.one_liner: Backward leakage through an incompetent aortic valve causes a wide pulse pressure, bounding neck pulses, and a diastolic murmur — often from valve dilation or cusp prolapse.
red_flags: Declining ejection fraction — surgical threshold for valve replacement

must_ask.say: Have you noticed your neck pulsing strongly, or your heartbeat feeling forceful?
Any breathlessness or chest pain with activity?
How long have you had this?

history.answer: I came in because I've been feeling a strong, pounding pulsation in my neck recently.
It feels like a heavy, forceful pounding rather than a fast racing beat, and I can actually see my neck vessels throbbing in the mirror.
It beats at a regular rhythm, just pounding much harder than it used to.
It came on gradually over the past several weeks and seems to be there almost constantly now.
I first noticed it about a month ago, and it has been getting progressively stronger and more bothersome.
The pounding is more noticeable when I exert myself or when I lie down flat on my left side at night.
Nothing really makes it stop, though resting quietly makes me feel a little more comfortable.
No, I have never fainted or felt like I was going to black out.
No, I haven't had any chest pain, tightness, or pressure.
I get mildly winded when I climb two flights of stairs, which used to be easy for me.
Yes, I've been feeling unusually worn out and fatigued lately, even after a full night's rest.
No, I don't have heat intolerance, excess sweating, or unexpected weight loss.
No, my hands don't tremble and I don't feel jittery.
No dizziness, my menstrual periods have been normal, and I haven't noticed any dark or black stools.
No pounding headaches, sudden cold sweats, or episodes of turning pale.
No, I haven't had any panic attacks, hyperventilation, or sudden feelings of impending doom.
No, I haven't had any fever, sore throat, or recent viral illness.
I drink one cup of coffee in the morning and never drink energy drinks.
I only have an occasional glass of wine when out with friends on weekends.
I don't take any prescription drugs, over-the-counter cold medicines, diet pills, or herbal supplements.
I have never been diagnosed with high blood pressure, a heart murmur, or any heart problem before.
No one in my family died suddenly at a young age or had heart failure, cardiomyopathy, or arrhythmias.
My past medical history has been completely unremarkable.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been hospitalized.
I do not have any allergies to medications or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
I work as an office manager and live with my husband in an apartment.
My last menstrual period was two weeks ago, my cycles are regular every 28 days, and I am not pregnant.
I thought the pounding in my neck was just from extreme stress and drinking too many energy drinks during my night shifts.
I'm terrified that one of the pulsing veins in my neck might burst and cause a sudden stroke while I'm alone in the house.
I'm hoping to get a medication today that will calm my racing heart and stop my neck from visibly throbbing.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 146/52 mmHg with wide pulse pressure, heart rate 76 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, body temperature 36.7 °C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Prominent visible carotid pulsations in the neck and a hyperdynamic apical impulse displaced slightly inferolaterally.
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor, and sclerae are clear and anicteric.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, non-tender, and smooth without palpable nodules or bruits.
No resting or postural tremor noted in the outstretched fingers.

Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; high-pitched, blowing early diastolic decrescendo murmur heard best at the left third intercostal space with the patient sitting upright and leaning forward in full expiration.
Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally with normal vesicular breath sounds and no crackles or wheezes.
Bounding, rapidly rising and collapsing peripheral pulses present bilaterally in the radial and carotid arteries.
No pitting edema noted over the pretibial areas or ankles bilaterally.
